lessons.limit: This lesson is an introductory comparison, not mastery of three large fields. The debates remain live; lack of consensus does not prove all answers equally good or that there is no right answer. Evaluate definitions, arguments, evidence, and value premises separately.
lessons.prompt: Compare a free-will question, an ethical question, and a meaning question about one choice. Identify the facts and the value premises separately.
recallKeys: I can distinguish compatibilist, libertarian, and skeptical positions without presenting one as settled.
I can distinguish a descriptive explanation from an ethical conclusion and identify its value premise.
I can explain how a question about meaning differs from a question about pleasure or causal explanation.

lessons.title: Existence and testing competing explanations
lessons.summary: Ask what exists, why there is anything at all, and how different kinds of explanation can be assessed.
paragraphs: Ontology asks what exists and what kinds of things there are. A rock, a number, an institution, and an experience raise different questions about existence. A deeper question is: why is there something rather than nothing? Suggested answers appeal to necessity, a creator, fundamental laws, or a brute fact without further explanation. Each invites objections; the course does not present one as established.

For empirical explanations, ask what each predicts and what observation would favor a rival. A cosmological account of how the universe developed is not automatically an answer to why any universe or laws exist. A physical vacuum is not philosophical nothingness: it belongs to a physical framework. Where proposals have no distinguishing observable consequences, empirical tests alone cannot choose between them; clarity, logical consistency, explanatory scope, and explicit assumptions still matter. Keeping these questions separate prevents confidence in a scientific model from becoming an unsupported claim about ultimate reality.

example.title: Illustrative example
example.text: Someone says that particles arising from a vacuum explain why anything exists. Ask what they mean by vacuum. If the account presupposes fields, laws, or a physical state, it may explain an event within an existing framework, not the absence of every framework. Another person proposes a necessary creator; ask why necessity applies there and what supports that premise. Neither a catchy scientific phrase nor a theological assertion settles the comparison without examining what each explanation actually assumes.

lessons.limit: There is no generally accepted answer to why anything exists. Empirical testability is crucial for scientific claims, but it is not the sole criterion for every philosophical or normative question. Lack of a test is not itself proof that a view is true, false, or meaningless.
lessons.prompt: Compare two answers to why there is something rather than nothing. State their assumptions, whether they make testable predictions, and what remains unexplained.
recallKeys: I can distinguish ontology from a scientific account of how an existing system changes.
I can explain why a physical vacuum is not philosophical nothingness.
I can compare two explanations by their assumptions and possible tests without claiming the question is settled.

lessons.title: The capstone: analyzing a real system with every tool
lessons.summary: Bring the whole course to bear on one real system, tracing its energy, incentives, power, and feedback together.
paragraphs: The final exercise applies this toolkit to one bounded system: a food supply chain, a city's housing, or a platform. Draw a map connecting at least four mechanisms rather than listing terms. Trace resources and energy, incentives and information, institutions and power, and feedback. For each important connection, record an observation or source, your proposed explanation, and how confident you are.

Now challenge the map. Identify a counterexample, an alternative explanation, and missing evidence. Specify a change that your model predicts and what result would make you revise it. Separate observations from causal inferences and judgments about fairness. Finally transfer the framework to an unfamiliar system: which mechanisms still fit, and which need replacing? Exposure is not mastery; explaining a mechanism, confronting contrary evidence, and applying it outside the original example provide a stronger self-check.

example.title: Illustrative example
example.text: Suppose you investigate local housing. Land and materials constrain supply; construction needs energy; developers respond to expected returns; planning rules distribute authority; and price expectations might reinforce speculation. Check planning records and other evidence rather than assuming this loop exists. Consider a rival explanation such as changing interest rates, and a counterexample where prices fell despite restricted building. Distinguish a claim about causation from your judgment about fairness. Then test the same framework on an unfamiliar system such as a water utility.

lessons.limit: No analysis is complete, and every real system has parts that resist these categories. The honest conclusion of the course is not mastery but a durable habit: ask what the model assumes, what the evidence says, what is being given up, and who bears the cost, and then update when the facts change.
lessons.prompt: Choose a real system and connect at least four mechanisms. Give evidence for each important link, distinguish observation from inference and value judgment, identify a counterexample and a rival explanation, then apply the framework to an unfamiliar system and state what you would change.
recallKeys: I can explain connections between at least four mechanisms using named evidence, not merely list concepts.
I can distinguish observation, causal inference, and value judgment, and state a counterexample or rival explanation.
I can apply the framework to an unfamiliar system and specify a prediction, missing evidence, or result that would change my model.
